headline: A perfect-severity Cisco auth bypass, a record Patch Tuesday, and a Defender bug with no patch
standfirst: Three new KEV entries, one of which is a 10.0; a record-shattering Microsoft release whose only real emergencies are two exploited Windows zero-days; and a Defender zero-day that yields SYSTEM on patched machines with no fix in sight. Two breach confirmations and an EU reporting clock that just got much shorter complete the picture.
bodyMarkdown:
## Actively exploited

Three new KEV entries landed, and only one should reorganise your queue: CVE-2026-20079, an authentication bypass in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center, scored 10.0 on CVSS 3.1. The vector is maximally hostile — network reachable, no privileges, no user interaction, scope changed, full confidentiality, integrity and availability impact, and root on the underlying operating system as the outcome. NVD attributes it to CWE-288, an improper system process created at boot time, with an unauthenticated remote attacker sending crafted HTTP requests to execute scripts and commands [[s22]]. The KEV entry covers FMC alongside Security Cloud Control Firewall Management, with vulnerable configurations listed across the 7.0.x releases and into 7.1.0.x. Required action is mitigation per vendor instructions under BOD 26-04, on a federal remediation deadline set only days after the addition. That deadline binds FCEB agencies; for everyone else it is a signal about how confidently the bug is being used. FMC is management-plane infrastructure — root there is a path to every firewall it controls. The same round covers a Citrix flaw and a Fortinet flaw whose details aren't in front of us, but edge and management kit is where KEV entries keep clustering.

Microsoft's record Patch Tuesday is the counterexample to treating volume as urgency. Roughly 974 flaws, 723 in Windows, 111 in Office and Office 2016, 62 in SQL, 22 in Developer Tools, over 110 rated critical — but only two confirmed as exploited in the wild, both Windows zero-days [[s47]]. The critical count tells you how big the release is; the exploited pair tells you what to do before the change window opens. Everything below that line is a capacity question, not an emergency.

## Vulnerabilities

Against that backdrop, the reported ShieldCrash exploit against Microsoft Defender deserves attention out of proportion to its documentation. It is described as a zero-day yielding full SYSTEM privileges on Windows machines that are current on their patches, with no fix available [[s28]]. Two things follow. A fully patched endpoint is not a trusted endpoint, which is the uncomfortable premise of every Defender-adjacent attack path. And with no CVE and no vendor patch, mitigation is entirely environmental: shrink the exposed surface, watch for anomalous SYSTEM-level process and script activity on hosts that have no business producing it, and assume the bug is circulating quietly before it is named. Zero-days in security products are attractive precisely because defenders trust the agent.

## Breaches

Two confirmations, both smaller in the telling than in the consequences. IDScan has confirmed attackers reached customer data in its cloud platform, days after reports tied it to a store of more than 153 million driver's license scans [[s1]]. The number is bad; the category is worse. Identity verification sits upstream of every other organisation's onboarding, and a licence scan cannot be reissued the way a password can. AdaptHealth confirmed 4.1 million people had health and insurance data exposed in an intrusion attributed to ShinyHunters [[s34]] — another entry in the long pattern where the intrusion is discovered well before the population is told. For both, the exploitable interval runs from compromise, not disclosure, and neither dataset improves with age.

## Industry

The Justice Department's action against Xinbi Guarantee is the most structurally interesting enforcement story in a while: Telegram channels seized, two cryptocurrency wallets taken, $52.8 million frozen, and the Scam Center Strike Force deployed to Madagascar against 13 compounds run by Chinese organised crime [[s41]]. Hitting the marketplace rather than the compounds targets the trust layer — the guarantee brand is what lets otherwise hostile operations transact — and freezing the crypto is the part that actually costs money. Separately, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act reporting duty takes effect imminently, giving organisations 24 hours to notify serious product security incidents [[s30]]. A day is not much time to establish scope, but it is solvable if disclosure is a rehearsed process rather than a scramble. Most programmes will find out that it isn't.

## Research

BlueMoon is the story that should shape your detection roadmap. The exploit kit chains multiple Windows and Chrome vulnerabilities, and its first in-the-wild use has been attributed to the China-aligned group tracked as APT31 — but within a week, four separate espionage-motivated clusters were using it [[s45]]. Fresh exploit capability is now a commodity that gets resold, leaked or copied faster than the underlying components can be patched individually. The takeaway isn't "patch Chrome faster" so much as "detect the chain": the value of a kit is in the sequence, and interrupting it anywhere defeats every group downstream of the original author.

nvd.description: The iDirect iQ200 does not validate CSRF tokens on state-changing API endpoints after authentication. The /api/reboot endpoint accepts POST requests authenticated solely by a session cookie that lacks the SameSite attribute. A remote attacker can host a malicious web page that, when visited by an authenticated administrator, automatically submits a cross-site POST request causing an immediate device reboot and satellite link loss. Repeated attacks can sustain a denial-of-service condition.

The iDirect iQ200 exposes the /api/identity and /api/ REST API endpoints without authentication. An unauthenticated attacker with network access can retrieve sensitive device information including the serial number, Device ID (DID), Terminal Private Key identifier (TPK), MAC address, and exact firmware version. The DID and TPK are used for satellite network authentication in the iDirect platform, potentially enabling terminal impersonation and network reconnaissance.

nvd.description: The vulnerability, if exploited, could allow a miscreant with read access to PIMBoards project files to decrypt and view sensitive information.

The vulnerability, if exploited, could allow an unauthenticated miscreant to perform read operations intended only for PIMBoards users, resulting in information disclosure. Write operations are not impacted.
The vulnerability, if exploited, could allow a miscreant to run arbitrary JavaScript code in a browser session of a PIMBoards user who was socially engineered to click on a malicious link.
